meetings.title: Interview: Senior Product Designer (Sofia Marin)
segments: Hi Sofia, welcome. Can you hear us okay?
Yes, perfectly. Hi Marcus, hi Maya. Thanks for having me.
Thanks for coming in. We've been looking forward to this.
Marcus has been talking about your portfolio all week.
Oh no, now I'm nervous. In a good way.
Hi Sofia, welcome. I'm Marcus, I lead design, and Maya leads product.
We'd love to start with a project from your portfolio, then we'll do a small critique exercise together.
Great. I'll walk you through the analytics redesign I led at a fintech company.
They had a dashboard with forty-two charts on the home page.
Nobody used it. Our research showed that people only looked at three of them, and even then mostly to check nothing was on fire.
What was your role on the project, specifically?
Were you the only designer?
I was the lead designer, with one other designer on the team.
I ran the research, set the direction, and designed the home page.
My colleague focused on the detail pages.
We had one PM and four engineers.
A small team. That matches how we work.
Forty-two charts. Wow.
So we redesigned the home around questions instead of charts.
'Is anything unusual today?', 'What changed this week?'.
Each question had one answer and a link to the detail.
Weekly active usage of the dashboard went from about fifteen percent to fifty-five percent.
How did you measure that fifty-five percent?
Weekly active on the dashboard page?
Weekly active users who opened the home page at least once, divided by all active users of the product.
We also tracked how often people clicked from a question into the detail, which went up almost four times.
That told us the answers were actually useful, not just visible.
Click-through to detail is a smart metric.
It separates looking from using.
How did you decide which questions?
Twenty interviews, and then a diary study for two weeks, where people logged every time they opened the dashboard and why.
The questions came straight from the diaries.
I didn't invent any of them.
What did the diary study tell you that interviews didn't?
Timing. In interviews, people said they checked the dashboard every morning.
The diaries showed they actually opened it when something felt wrong, usually after an angry email.
So the home page needed to answer 'is this the thing that's wrong', not give a morning overview.
That's a great insight. People describe their ideal selves in interviews.
Exactly. Diaries catch what people actually do.
I love that. How did you handle the power users who wanted the forty-two charts back?
We kept an 'all charts' view one click away, and we tracked it.
After two months, it was under five percent of sessions, so we stopped maintaining half of the charts.
How did you get engineering on board with removing charts? That's usually a fight.
Data. We showed that twenty of the charts had fewer than ten views a month, and several of them were expensive to compute.
Removing them made the page load twice as fast.
Engineering loved it once they saw that.
Did anyone complain loudly when the charts disappeared?
One team did, the finance analysts.
They used four specific charts every month for a report.
We rebuilt those four as a saved view just for them.
It took a day, and they became some of our biggest fans.
Listening to the loud minority without letting them drive everything. That's hard to do.
Okay, the exercise. I'll share a screen from our current work.
It's an early version of our themes home.
Talk us through your honest reaction.
First reaction, it's much calmer than most analytics products, which I like.
My main question is the growth arrow.
Growth relative to what? Last week?
Last month? And is a theme growing from two to four comments shown the same as one growing from two hundred to four hundred?
Would you show a trend at all for very small themes?
Probably not. Below some threshold, I'd just say 'new' or 'emerging', without an arrow.
A theme with four comments doesn't have a trend, it has a story, and the story is in the quotes.
'Emerging' is a nice word for it.
That's a great question. Right now, yes, they look the same.
I'd make the time period explicit, and I'd weight the arrow by volume, or at least show the absolute numbers on hover.
Otherwise small themes will look alarming and people will stop trusting the arrows.
If you had to pick one thing to test first, what would it be?
The arrow. Because it's the thing that could damage trust fastest.
If people see alarming arrows on tiny themes a couple of times, they'll ignore all the arrows, including the ones that matter.
That's a strong argument. Trust is our whole problem with the old tagging too.
Second, the quotes are the most human part of the card, but they're at the bottom.
I'd test moving one quote up, right under the label.
Anything else you'd push back on?
The count. '412 comments' is meaningful to you, but a new user doesn't know if 412 is a lot.
I'd show it relative to their total, like 'eight percent of all feedback this week'.
That makes the ranking self-explanatory.
Oh, I like that a lot.
And I'd test the label wording.
Some of these are quite abstract.
'Onboarding friction' versus 'Can't find the import button'.
The second one is something a team can act on.
How would you test label wording?
It's generated by the model, so it changes all the time.
I'd pick twenty real themes, write three versions of each label, the model's, a shorter one, and a problem-focused one, and ask people which one they'd act on.
Then feed the winning style back into the prompt as examples.
And we'd learn which style customers trust, which matters as much as which one they act on.
Exactly. Trust and action are related, but they're not the same thing. I'd measure both.
That's basically what Priya and I were planning, but more rigorous.
What would worry you about working on a product like ours?
Honestly, I haven't worked much on admin and enterprise settings.
Permissions, SSO setup, that kind of thing.
I know it matters for your customers, and I'd need to ramp up there.
How do you usually get up to speed in a new domain?
I shadow support for a week.
Reading tickets tells you where people get stuck much faster than any documentation.
For enterprise settings, I'd also ask to sit in on a few implementation calls with IT teams.
That's exactly what we'd want.
Our support team would love you.
What does the design team look like today?
Three designers including me, and a researcher we share with marketing.
You'd own the insights and themes area end to end, and work very closely with Priya on how the AI shows up in the interface.
That's exciting. AI interfaces are where I want to spend the next few years.
That's an honest answer, thank you.
Thanks Sofia. We'll be in touch about next steps this week.
Before we go, can I ask a question?
How do designers and the ML team work together today?
Closely, but informally. Priya and I sit down every week or so.
Honestly, I'd love someone to make that more deliberate, especially around how the AI explains itself in the interface.
That's the part of the job I'd be most excited about.
Thank you, Sofia. This was a great conversation.
